goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
goldens.reasoning: C1 points at the same code, should_block? updating match_count statistics, and the race condition it causes. The golden comment also calls out the side effect in a read method, which C1 touches on.

goldens.comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
goldens.reasoning: C2 identifies the same missing anchor in the @(#{domains}) regex that enables a whitelist bypass. Its example is a different domain shape, but the underlying flaw is the same.

goldens.comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
goldens.reasoning: No candidate mentions the case-sensitive email lookup.

candidates: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) reads match_count, increments it in Ruby, then saves — if two requests race, one increment is lost because both read the same value before either saves. Should use increment!(:match_count) for atomic SQL update instead.

The regex @(#{domains}) lacks an end-of-string anchor, so user@allowed.com.malicious.org passes whitelist validation when only allowed.com is whitelisted. The pattern matches @allowed.com as a substring anywhere in the domain. Need to add \z to anchor to the end of the email address.
